newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks end lower after big rally falters.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks end lower after big rally falters.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks staged a blistering rally Tuesday, rising more than 100 points on mild inflation news before profit-taking wiped out all of the gains in late trading to send the Dow Jones industrial average to its fifth consecutive loss.
Bonds gave up most of their gains to end modestly higher, and the dollar ended higher, but off its peak against the Japanese yen.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended down 4.61 points at 6,656.08. The blue-chip index has now fallen for five straight sessions, the first time it has done so since last June.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,399 to 1,030 on heavy volume of 526 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The stock market tracked the volatile session in bonds, where a rally of more than a full point in the Treasury's key 30-year bond also lost steam.

At the close, the long-bond held a small gain of 6/32, or $1.875 on a $1,000 bond, which trimmed its yield to 6.93 percent from 6.94 percent on Monday. Early in the session, the yield, which moves in the opposite direction of the bond's price, hovered at 6.83 percent.

Financial markets exploded from the start on news that the Employment Cost Index -- a key indicator of wage price pressure -- rose 0.8 percent in the last three months of 1996, slightly less than the 0.9 percent that Wall Street had expected, quashing fears of a dangerous inflationary spike.
The Labour Department reported that U.S. workers' compensation in the fourth quarter rose 0.8 percent after a 0.6 percent gain in the third quarter.
"The ECI started the day off well and said there is no current danger of inflation even with the unemployment rate as low as it is," said Stan Shipley, senior strategist at Lehman Brothers.
Later, however, strong retail sales and consumer confidence data eroded the bond market's rally and triggered stiff profit-taking in stocks.

"The ECI was a good excuse for a bounce and there was a lot of short covering going on early," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "But when people saw the market up 100 points and (bond) yields starting to work back up towards 7 percent, the bounce got sold."

The dollar ended the day at 120.95 yen, up from 119.57 late Monday. It reached a peak of 121.77 yen during the session, its highest level since February 1993, buoyed also by evidence that the world's major industrial nations remain content with the dollar's current strength.
Against the mark, the dollar retreated from sharp early gains to close little changed at 1.6470 vs. 1.6473 late Monday. Early Tuesday it reached a high of 1.6570 marks, its top level since June 1994.

Gold and silver prices tumbled because higher stock prices may siphon investor support away from the metals. February gold at the New York Mercantile Exchange's Comex divsion ended down $3.30 an ounce at $354.00, and March silver ended down 8.4 cents an ounce Tuesday at $4.963.
Wheat prices rose ahead of expected sales to Egypt and India, while orange juice rose again on worries of freeze damage in Florida.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat for March delivery closed up 1-1/2 cents at $3.73 per bushel.
Frozen concentrated orange juice prices closed higher at New York's Cotton Exchange as fears persisted that a recent cold spell damaged Florida oranges.
The March orange juice contract closed up 0.25 cent to 93.75 cents a pound after earlier peaking at 99.00, the highest level since Dec. 5.

Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index closed 25.4 points higher at 4,237.4, carried up by a buoyant Dow which was 93 points higher as London closed. In Tokyo, the key Nikkei 225 average finished up 461.67 points, or 2.66 percent, at 17,796.57.
